claims.text: An HPA only updates the scale target's replica count; the Deployment's ReplicaSet creates the Pods, and each new Pod is then placed on a node by kube-scheduler.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (scale subresource); Kubernetes Scheduler

claims.text: kube-scheduler places a Pod only on a node where the node's allocatable resources minus the sum of the requests of Pods already on it cover the Pod's requests; actual use by those Pods is not considered.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Resource Management for Pods and Containers > How Pods with resource requests are scheduled; Reserve Compute Resources for System Daemons (Node Allocatable)

claims.text: Phase Pending: accepted by the API server, containers not yet running; an unscheduled Pod stays Pending. When kube-scheduler finds no fitting node it records a FailedScheduling event on the Pod giving reasons per node (e.g. Insufficient cpu); kubectl can show events.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Pod Lifecycle > Pod phase (Pending); Resource Management > My Pod is pending with event message FailedScheduling

claims.text: A cluster autoscaler watches for Pods unschedulable for lack of resources and, when nodes from a group's template would fit them, has the provider add as many as needed to make them schedulable, within the group's configured limits; it acts on requests, not CPU use.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Node Autoscaling (Cluster Autoscaler: provisioning triggered by unschedulable Pods); Cluster Autoscaler FAQ: How does scale-up work?

claims.text: A provisioned node is backed by a provider resource, most commonly a VM, which must be created, boot and register before kube-scheduler places Pods on it; so it takes longer than placing a Pod on an existing node with room. Waiting Pods stay Pending.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Node Autoscaling (resources backing Nodes, most commonly VMs); Nodes > Self-registration of Nodes

claims.text: A cluster autoscaler removes a node when its Pods' requests are low and all of them can be placed on other nodes; it evicts those Pods, as a drain does, and their controllers recreate them on other nodes.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Node Autoscaling > Consolidation; Cluster Autoscaler FAQ: How does scale-down work?

claims.text: kind runs each node as a Docker container, created with the cluster from deploy/k8s/kind-config.yaml (one control plane, two workers); nothing in donhang adds nodes afterwards, so the node count stays fixed.
claims.source_hint: kind docs: Quick Start > Configuring Your kind Cluster (nodes); examples/don-hang STAGE.md stage-4 'Clusters and their resources'

claims.text: In a multi-node kind cluster the control-plane node keeps the node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane NoSchedule taint, so ordinary Pods are not placed on it (the '1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s)' part of the event).
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Well-Known Labels, Annotations and Taints (node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane); kind docs (control-plane taint removed only for single-node clusters)

claims.text: The rest of the FailedScheduling message after the per-node reasons is about scheduler features beyond node fit; its 'preemption: ...' part concerns Pod priority.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Pod Priority and Preemption

claims.text: node-capacity.sh @ stage-4: sets cpu-echo's CPU request to 60% of a worker's allocatable CPU (24-37), patches minReplicas to 4 (40-62), prints a Pending Pod's FailedScheduling event (64-76), then restores minReplicas 1, request 50m, deletes autoscale-lessons.

node-capacity.sh stops with exit 1 if a worker has less than 60% of its CPU unrequested, printing 'delete earlier lessons' namespaces first'; lessons_cluster creates donhang if missing; show (scripts/lib/network-lessons.sh) prints and runs a command.

Captured output: HPA cpu-echo cpu: <unknown>/50%, MINPODS 4, REPLICAS 4; Deployment 2/4 ready; Pending: 2, Running: 2; event '0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 2 Insufficient cpu...'.

capacity-plan.md 44-54 @ stage-4: each api Pod holds an Npgsql pool; other services, migrations, backups use the same server; Pods × connections per Pod over all services < max_connections (SHOW max_connections); headroom: peak ≤ half the ceiling of 2 api Pods.

PostgreSQL's max_connections caps concurrent connections to the server and is read with SHOW max_connections; adding Kubernetes nodes does not change it. An Npgsql pool keeps open connections and reuses them, up to a maximum pool size.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 19.3 Connections and Authentication > max_connections; SHOW; Npgsql docs: Connection String Parameters > Pooling (Maximum Pool Size)

claims.text: A ResourceQuota can make the API server refuse new Pods of a namespace that would exceed it, independent of node capacity.

Opinion: on machines the team runs itself, buy nodes for the planned peak plus headroom and keep maxReplicas within what they hold by requests; with a gradual peak on a managed cluster, pair an HPA with a cluster autoscaler and rely on the plan's headroom while nodes start.

Opinion: for a sharp peak at a known time, HPA + cluster autoscaler react too late on their own (a node takes Pods only after its machine is created and booted); raise minReplicas by a commit before it so nodes join in time, and lower it after.
claims.source_hint: trade-off reasoning (node start-up time vs. peak onset)

claims.text: Opinion (trade-offs table): nodes bought ahead cost the peak's capacity all day but have room at once; a cluster autoscaler pays for nodes matching placed requests but new Pods wait while a node starts, and needs a provider that creates nodes on request.
claims.source_hint: trade-off reasoning; Kubernetes docs: Node Autoscaling
